rib.e: From Middle English rib, ribbe, from Old English ribb (“rib”), from Proto-West Germanic *ribi, from Proto-Germanic *ribją (“rib, reef”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rebʰ- (“arch, ceiling, cover”).
rib.g: Any of a series of long curved bones occurring in 12 pairs in humans and other animals and extending from the spine to or toward the sternum

rib.e: From Middle English ribbe, from Old English ribbe (“hound's-tongue”).

ribband.g: A long, narrow strip of timber bent and bolted longitudinally to the ribs of a vessel, to hold them in position and give rigidity to the fra

ribbon.e: From Middle English riban, ryban, ryband, from Old French riban, ruban ( > modern French ruban), of uncertain origin. Likely from a Germanic compound whose second element is cognate with English band.
ribbon.g: A long, narrow strip of material used for decoration of clothing or the hair or gift wrapping.

rich.e: From Middle English riche (“strong, powerful, rich”), from Old English rīċe (“powerful, mighty, great, high-ranking, rich, wealthy, strong, potent”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīkī (“powerful, rich”), from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz (“kingly, powerful, rich”), from Proto-Germanic *rīks (“king, ruler”), an early borrowing from Proto-Celtic *rīxs.
rich.g: Wealthy: having a lot of money and possessions.

riches.e: From Middle English riches, plural of riche (“power, wealth”), from Old English rīċe (“power, authority, dominion”). Confused with Middle English richesse (“wealth”), from Old French richesse, from riche (“rich, wealthy”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *rīki (“rich”) from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz (“rich, powerful”).
From rich + -es (plural suffix) by analogy with poors (“poor people”).

richly.e: From Middle English richely, from Old English rīċlīċe, from Proto-West Germanic *rīkīlīkō, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijalīkô; by surface analysis, rich + -ly (adverbial suffix).
richly.g: In a luxurious manner; full of majesty or expression:

richness.e: From Middle English richenesse; by surface analysis, rich + -ness.
richness.g: The state or quality of being rich; wealthiness, wealth, riches.

riddance.e: Apparently an alteration of earlier Middle English riddeings, ryddyngs, reddyngs (“clearings, clearances”), plural of riddyng, riddynge, rudyng (“clearing away, removal”), partially continuing Old English hryding (“a clearing, cleared land”), by surface analysis, rid + -ance.
riddance.g: An act of ridding, clearance, or removal; elimination.

riddle.e: From Middle English redel, redels, from Old English rǣdels, rǣdelse (“counsel, opinion, imagination, riddle”), from Proto-West Germanic *rādislī (“counsel, conjecture”). Analyzable as rede (“advice”) + -le.
riddle.g: A verbal puzzle, mystery, or other problem of an intellectual nature.

riddle.e: From Middle English riddel, ridel, redel, rudel, from Old French ridel ("a plaited stuff; curtain"; > Medieval Latin ridellus), from rider (“to wrinkle”), from Old High German rīdan (“to turn; wrap; twist; wrinkle”).

ride.e: From Middle English riden, from Old English rīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīdan, from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną (“to ride”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreydʰ- (“to ride”), from *h₃reyH- (“to move”), from *h₃er- (“to move, stir”).
ride.g: To transport oneself by sitting on and directing a horse, later also a bicycle etc.

rider.e: From Middle English ryder, ridere, from Late Old English rīdere (“rider, knight”). By surface analysis, ride + -er.

ridge.e: From Middle English rigge, rygge, (also rig, ryg, rug), from Old English hryċġ (“back, spine, ridge, elevated surface”), from Proto-West Germanic *hrugi, from Proto-Germanic *hrugjaz (“back”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krewk-, *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”).
ridge.g: The back of any animal; especially the upper or projecting part of the back of a quadruped.

ridicule.e: The obsolete adjective is borrowed from French ridicule, from Latin rīdiculus (“laughable, comical, amusing, absurd, ridiculous”), from ridere (“to laugh”).
ridicule.g: To criticize or disapprove of someone or something through scornful jocularity; to make fun of.

ridicule.e: Apparently from French ridicule (“reticule”), probably a punning alteration of réticule after ridicule (“ridicule”).
ridicule.g: A small woman's handbag; a reticule.

riding.e: From Middle English rydyng; equivalent to ride + -ing.

rifle.e: Originally short for “rifled gun”, referring to the spiral grooves inside the barrel. From Middle English riflen (“to rob, plunder, search through”), from Old French rifler (“to lightly scratch, scrape off, plunder”).
rifle.g: A firearm fired from the shoulder; improved range and accuracy is provided by a long, rifled barrel.

right.e: From Middle English reȝt, right, righte, riht, riȝt, riȝte, ryght, ryȝt, from Old English reht, reoht, rieht, riht, ryht (“right,” also the word for “straight” and “direct”), from Proto-West Germanic *reht, from Proto-Germanic *rehtaz (“right, straight; just, morally upright”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós (“right, straightened”).
right.g: Designating the side of the body which is positioned to the east if one is facing north, the side on which the heart is not located in most

right.e: From Middle English right, righte, from Old English rihte, rehte (“right; rightly; due; directly; straight”), from Proto-Germanic *rehta, from *rehtaz (“right; straight”).

righteous.e: From earlier rightuous, rightwose, rightwos, rightwise, from Middle English rightwise, rightwis, from Old English rihtwīs (“righteous, just”), corresponding to right + -wise (with assimilation of second element to -ous), or to right + wise (“way, manner”).

righteously.e: From Middle English rightwisly, from Old English rihtwīslīce; equivalent to righteous + -ly.

righteousness.e: Corruption of earlier rightwiseness, from Middle English rightwisnes, from Old English rihtwīsnes (“justice”). By surface analysis, righteous + -ness.
righteousness.g: The quality or state of being righteous.

rightful.e: From Middle English rightful, ryghtfull, riȝtful, from Old English *rihtfull (suggested by derivative unrihtfull (“unrightful”)), equivalent to right + -ful.

rightly.e: From Middle English ryȝtly, rihtliche, from Old English rihtlīċe, from Proto-West Germanic *rehtalīkā, *rehtalīkō, from Proto-Germanic *rehtalīkê, *rehtalīkô (“rightly”), equivalent to right + -ly.
rightly.g: In a right manner; correctly, justifiably.

rigid.e: From Middle English rigide, from Latin rigidus (“stiff”), from rigeō (“to be stiff”). Merged with Middle English rigged, rygged, rugged (“upright like a spine, rigid”, literally “ridged”).

rigour.e: From Middle English rigour, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French rigor, from Latin rigor (“stiffness, rigidity, rigor, cold, harshness”), from rigere (“to be rigid”).

rile.e: From a dialectal pronunciation of roil.
rile.g: To stir or move from a state of calm or order.

rim.e: From Middle English rim, rym, rime, from Old English rima (“rim, edge, border, bank, coast”), from Proto-Germanic *rimô, *rembô (“edge, border”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *rem-, *remə- (“to rest, support, be based”).
rim.g: An edge around something, especially when circular.

rim.e: From Middle English rim, rym, ryme, reme, from Old English rēoma (“membrane, ligament”), from Proto-West Germanic *reumō.

ring.e: From Middle English ryng, from Old English hring (“ring, circle”), from Proto-West Germanic *hring, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz (“ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krengʰ-, extended nasalized form of *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”).
ring.g: A solid object in the shape of a circle.

ring.e: From Middle English ryngen, from Old English hrinġan (“to ring”), from Proto-West Germanic *hringijan, from Proto-Germanic *hringijaną (“to ring”), of imitative origin.
ring.g: The resonant sound of a bell, or a sound resembling it.

ringleader.g: A leader of a group of people, especially an unofficial group.

rinse.e: From Middle English rinsen, rincen, rencen (“to rinse”), from Old French rincier, reinser, Old Northern French raïncer (“to rinse, cleanse”). Of contested origin. Possibly from Old Norse hreinsa, from Proto-Germanic *hrainisōną (“to clean, purify”), from Proto-Indo-European *krey- (“to separate, divide”).
rinse.g: To wash (something) quickly using water and no soap.

riot.e: From Middle English riot (“debauched living, dissipation”), from Old French riote (“debate”), from rioter (“to quarrel”), perhaps related to riboter or from Latin rugio (“to roar”).
riot.g: A tumultuous disturbance of the public peace by a large group of people, often involving violence or damage to property.

riotous.e: From Middle English riotous, from Anglo-Norman riotous; equivalent to riot + -ous.
riotous.g: Having the characteristics of a riot.

rip.e: From Middle English rippen, from earlier ryppen (“to pluck”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rupjaną and/or *ruppōną, intensive of *raupijaną, causative of Proto-Indo-European *Hrewp- (“to break”). Possible doublet of rub.
rip.g: To divide or separate the parts of (especially something flimsy, such as paper or fabric), by cutting or tearing; to tear off or out by viol

rip.e: Uncertain; perhaps a variant of rep (“reprobate”).

ripe.e: From Middle English ripe, rype, from Old English rīpe (“ripe, mature”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīpī, from Proto-Germanic *rīpijaz, *rīpiz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reyb- (“to snatch”).
ripe.g: Of a fruit, vegetable, seed, etc., ready for reaping or gathering; having attained perfection; mature.

ripe.e: From Middle English ripe, from Latin ripa.

ripen.e: From Middle English *ripenen, extended form of ripen, from Old English rīpian. In the modern form, equivalent to ripe + -en (inchoative and factitive suffix). As in several other verbs, the alteration seems to have occurred during the time when the infinitive and plural ending -en was in the process of being lost (and was thus open to reinterpretation).
ripen.g: Of grain, fruit, flowers, etc., to grow ripe; to become mature.

rise.e: From Middle English risen, from Old English rīsan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīsan, from Proto-Germanic *rīsaną (“to rise”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rey- (“to arise, rise”). According to Kroonen (2013), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er- (“to rise, spring”).
rise.g: To move, or appear to move, physically upwards relative to the ground.

rise.e: From Middle English ris, rys, from Old English hrīs, from Proto-Germanic *hrīsą (“twig; shoot”).

risk.e: From earlier risque, from Middle French risque, from Old Italian risco (“risk”) (modern Italian rischio) and rischiare (“to run into danger”).
risk.g: The probability of a negative outcome to a decision or event.

rite.e: Via Middle English and Old French, from Latin ritus.

rival.e: Borrowed from Latin rīvālis (literally “person using the same stream as another”). By surface analysis, Latin rīvus + -al.
rival.g: A competitor (person, team, company, etc.) with the same goal as another, or striving to attain the same thing. Defeating a rival may be a p

river.e: From Middle English ryver, from Anglo-Norman rivere, from Early Medieval Latin rīpāria (“littoral, riverbank”), from Latin rīpārius (“of a riverbank”), from Latin rīpa (“river bank”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reyp- (“to scratch, tear, cut”). Unrelated to Latin rīvus (“stream”) (whence rival, derive). Largely displaced native English ea.
river.g: A large and often winding stream which drains a land mass, carrying water down from higher areas to a lower point, oftentimes ending in anot

riverbed.g: The path where a river runs, or where a river once ran; the bottom earthen part of a river, not including the riverbanks.
